BMC Anesthesiology
Ivabradine use in critical care: a systematic 
review and metanalysis of cardiogenic 
and septic shock patients
Lorenzo Antonino Calabrò1*, Marco Pasetto2,3, Sabino Scolletta4, Filippo Annoni1, Zoe Demailly5, 
Katarina Halenarova1
, Katia Donadello2,6 and Fabio Silvio Taccone1
Abstract
Introduction In patients with acute illness, compensatory tachycardia initially serves to maintain adequate cardiac 
output, oxygen delivery and tissue oxygenation but may persist despite appropriate fluid and vasopressor resuscitation or may be secondary to inotropic therapy. Sustained tachycardia is a predictor of adverse outcomes in critical illness. Ivabradine, a highly selective inhibitor of the sinoatrial node’s pacemaker current (If
 or "funny" current), mitigates 
tachycardia by modulating diastolic depolarization slope without affecting contractility.

Aim To report the existing evidence on the use of ivabradine in critically ill patients and assess its effect on rate control.
Methods A systematic literature search was performed up to May 2024 in the MEDLINE/PubMed®, Cochrane Controlled Clinical Trial register, EMBASE® and Scopus® databases. The search included: P- only original studies conducted 
in humans admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU); I – when ivabradine administration was tested; C – in presence 
or absence of a control group; O – for any outcome; S – including case reports, randomized and observational trials, 
published in English in peer-reviewed journals.
Results After the first screening, 39 studies were assessed for eligibility on a total of 682 records identified. Among 
those, 29 were excluded; 10 studies (4 randomized controlled trial, 5 case report/series, 1 prospective observational), 
including a total of 243 patients, were included in the qualitative analysis, 6 studies were included in the quantitative 
analysis. The use of ivabradine resulted in a pooled mean heart rate reduction of 18.70 [12.70–24.80] bpm (p<0.01) 
without a significant decrease in cardiac index (p=0.59). A significant reduction of noradrenaline dose was reported 
in one study (-0.134 mcg/kg/min; 95% CI -0.172 to -0.012; p=0.027). In addition, the combination of dobutamine 
with ivabradine has been reported to optimize dobutamine inotropic action, while mitigating its positive chronotropic effects, resulting in a more efficient cardiac cycle and improved hemodynamics.
Conclusions Ivabradine may be a useful alternative to beta-blocker in the management of inappropriate sinus 
tachycardia. Yet, evidence is limited and inconsistent. Larger randomized trials are needed to investigate the potential 
benefits or hazards of ivabradine use on hemodynamics and long-term outcomes.
Keywords Ivabradine, Critically illness, Shock, Clinical studies

Introduction
Tachycardia is a common trait of acute circulatory failure 
[1]; while it initially serves to maintain adequate cardiac 
output, oxygen delivery and tissue oxygenation, tachycardia may persist over time despite appropriate fluid and 
vasopressor resuscitation or may result from inotropic 
therapy [2]. In patients with septic shock, persistent tachycardia was associated with higher probability of death 
[3], yet beta-blockers showed no effect on outcome, with 
concerns of possible harm due to their negative effect on 
myocardial contractility [4]. In patients with low cardiac 
output during cardiogenic shock or after cardiac surgery, 
dobutamine is administered to improve contractility and 
cardiac output [5]. Yet, it can induce persistent tachycardia, with negative effects on myocardial metabolism, 
cardiac efficiency and is associated with a higher risk of 
arrhythmias [6].
Ivabradine is an approved drug for chronic heart failure 
with reduced ejection fraction, serving as an adjunct to 
beta-blockers for rate control [7]. It is available in pills to 
be administered twice daily for a 2 h main half-life and 
11 h effective half-life. This drug targets the sinoatrial 
node"funny"currents (If) channels [8], responsible for its 
pacemaker activity. By interacting only with the active 
state of the channel, ivabradine can reduce heart rate 
without causing severe bradycardia. Unlike beta-blockers and calcium channel antagonists, ivabradine does 
not exhibit negative inotropic effects [9], making its use 
appealing in patients with impaired contractility, acute 
circulatory failure, and multi-organ dysfunction. However, the data available in these patients remain limited.
We therefore conducted a systematic review of the 
literature to report the existing evidence on the use of 
ivabradine in critically ill patients.
Methods
We adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis—Protocols (PRISMA-P) 
guidelines [10]. The protocol of this study was registered

with the International Prospective Register of Systematic 
Reviews PROSPERO n CRD42023449267.
Data sources and search strategies
A systematic literature search was performed up to the 
20/04/25 in the MEDLINE/PubMed®, Cochrane Controlled 
Clinical Trial register, EMBASE® and Scopus® databases. The 
search included: P- only original studies conducted in humans 
admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU), published in English 
in peer-reviewed journals; I – when ivabradine administration 
was tested; C – in presence or absence of a control group; O – 
for any outcome; S – including case reports, randomized and 
observational trials. The following keywords and their related 
MeSh terms were used:"ivabradine","critical care","intensive 
care","sepsis","septic shock","shock","cardiogenic shock",
"cardiac surgery","ECMO","extra-corporeal membrane 
oxygenation","mechanical circulatory support","Acute systolic dysfunction","acute ventricular dysfunction","atrial 
fibrillation","arrythmia","multi-organ dysfunction", with filters 
for language (English). In addition, we searched the reference 
lists of eligible studies and relevant reviews for additional published and unpublished data, searched by contacting experts, 
and used a web search for abstracts, proceedings, and unpublished studies.
Study screening and selection
The studies were independently screened by two authors 
(LC and MP), looking at study titles and abstracts for 
potential eligibility. Additional citations were also identified by the authors of the present review based on their 
prior knowledge of the literature. Disagreement between 
authors was assessed and resolved through a third senior reviewer (FA), who reviewed the original text of the 
article. None of the authors of the original studies was 
contacted to obtain further information, which were not 
available in the published manuscript.
Appraisal of study quality
The level of evidence (LOE) of each study was assessed 
according to the Risk Of Bias In Non randomized Studies 
– of Interventions (ROBINS-I) [11] for non-randomized

studies and according to Risk of Bias 2 (RoB2) [12] tool 
for randomized studies. We selected relevant risk of bias 
indicators, and we evaluated risk of bias regarding confounding, population selection, intervention classification, deviation from intended intervention, missing data, 
measurement of outcomes, selection of reported results. 
The included trials were judged as “low risk of bias” when 
all domains were judged as low risk of bias. Trials were 
judged as “moderate risk of bias” when moderate risk of 
bias was judged in one to two domains. Conversely, trials 
were judged as “high risk of bias” when high risk of bias 
was judged in one or more domains or when moderate 
risk of bias was judged in more than two domains. LOE 
was further analyzed by two experts (LC and MP). Disagreement was resolved by consensus.
Statistical analysis
Statistical analysis was conducted on the summary statistics described in the selected articles (e.g., means, 
medians, proportions). Means of heart rate and cardiac 
index before and after ivabradine administration were 
obtained by weighting each study by the inverse of variance. Mantel–Haenszel method was chosen as the reference method for fixed effects analysis. Z test was carried 
out to assess the significance of the risk differences. The 
I2 was calculated by χ2 test to assess variability due to 
Calabrò et al. BMC Anesthesiology (2025) 25:276 Page 3 of 10
heterogeneity rather than chance. I2 values around 25%, 
50%, and 75% represented low, moderate, and high heterogeneity; 95% CI for heart rate and cardiac index were 
calculated with the Wilson method and placed in forest 
plots and statistical significance was assumed for p< 0.05. 
The presence of publication bias was evaluated by trim 
and fill. The trim and fill method estimates the number of 
missing studies from a meta-analysis due to the suppression of the most extreme results on one side of the funnel 
plot. Then, this method augments the observed data and

recomputes the summary estimate based on the complete data. The trim and fill outputs were obtained with 
iterations. Statistical analysis was conducted by Review 
Manager 5.3 software and funnel and forest plots were 
developed.
Results
Study selection and characteristics
A total of 6537records were identified after the initial 
research. After the first screening procedure, 39 studies were assessed for eligibility (Fig.  1). Among these, 
29 were excluded; a total of 10 studies, including 243 
patients, were included for the initial qualitative analysis. 
Six were included in the quantitative analysis [13–18]. 
Four studies were randomized control trials investigating 
Fig. 1 Flowchart of included studies. LCOS, low cardiac output syndrome; MODS, multiorgan dysfunction; RCT, randomized controlled trial
Calabrò et al. BMC Anesthesiology (2025) 25:276 Page 4 of 10
effect of ivabradine in low cardiac output syndrome after 
cardiac surgery (LCOS) [17], cardiogenic shock secondary to acute myocardial ischemia [13], septic shock [15] 
and multi-organ dysfunction [18], respectively (Fig.  1). 
Five studies were case reports about ivabradine use during mechanical circulatory support [14], LCOS [10], 
heart transplantation [19], cardiogenic shock secondary 
to myocarditis [20], sepsis-related multi-organ dysfunction [21], and one prospective observational trial on cardiogenic shock [16] respectively. Among the randomized, 
two studies were judged of low risk [15, 17] and two of 
moderate risk of bias [13, 18]. Among the non-randomized, four studies were judged of moderate risk and 
two of high risk of bias [14, 21] (Figs. 2 and 3).
Heart rate and cardiac index before and after ivabradine 
administration
Six studies reported means heart rate before and after 
ivabradine administration with a total of 146 patients 
included. Ivabradine administration was associated with 
a mean heart rate reduction of 18.70 bpm [12.60; 24.80]

(p < 0.01), Significant heterogeneity was found among 
studies (I2= 86%) (Fig. 4).
Four studies reported means cardiac index before and 
after ivabradine administration with a total of 86 patients 
included. Ivabradine administration was not associated a significant change in cardiac index (−0.03 L/min/
m2
 [−0.16; 0.09]; p< 0.01), Significant heterogeneity was 
found among studies (I2= 80%) (Fig. 5).
Main Results
A phase 1 trial was conducted on 60 patients with septic shock, exhibiting a persistent heart rate of 95 bpm or 
higher [15]. The treatment group experienced a statistically significant increase in indexed stroke volume (+
5.849 ml/m2
; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.293–10.5; 
p= 0.017), accompanied by a reduction in heart rate 
(−25.57 bpm; 95% CI −31.45 to −15.88; p< 0.001) and 
decreased vasopressor requirement (−0.134 mcg/kg/
min; 95% CI −0.172 to −0.012; p= 0.027). Furthermore, 
the 96-h survival rate was higher in the treatment group, 
while no difference in 90-day mortality was observed. 
Similar positive outcomes were reported in a case series 
of 3 patients presenting with septic shock and multiorgan dysfunction following cardiac surgery [21].
In a phase two multicenter trial, the addition of ivabradine to dobutamine treatment was studied in patients 
with post-cardiac surgery low cardiac output syndrome

and a heart rate higher than 100 bpm [17]. Compared to 
dobutamine infusion alone, ivabradine administration led 
to a significant reduction in heart rate within one hour,

accompanied by increased cardiac output, stroke volume, and systolic blood pressure. This allowed clinicians 
to safely increase dobutamine dosage in 43% of patients 
to achieve hemodynamic targets, according to authors. 
Similar positive results were observed in a case series of 
15 patients with low cardiac output syndrome following on-pump cardiac surgery [21]. In a case involving a 
37-year-old cardiac transplant patient with acute renal 
insufficiency and persistent sinus tachycardia of up to 120 
bpm, ivabradine successfully controlled heart rate and led 
to an increase in cardiac output, discontinuation of inotropes, and resolution of acute renal insufficiency [18].
Barillà et  al. conducted a preliminary randomized 
open-label control trial to investigate the use of ivabradine as an adjuvant therapy during cardiogenic shock 
of ischemic origin [13]. Patients in the ivabradine group 
experienced a significant reduction in heart rate (−10.3± 
6 bpm; p< 0.001), along with elevated arterial systolic (3.6 
±3.5 mmHg; p< 0.001) and diastolic pressures (2.9 ±4.5 
mmHg; p< 0.001) up to six months after the acute event. 
Additionally, a noteworthy increase in ejection fraction 
(4.1 ±2.5%; p< 0.0005) was observed three months after 
the event. In a case report involving two patients with 
cardiogenic shock due to myocarditis and presenting 
with tachycardia up to 120 bpm during inotrope infusion 
[10], a resolution of tachycardia and gradual weaning 
from inotropes following daily ivabradine administration 
was observed.
A prospective non randomized trial investigated the 
use of ivabradine during cardiogenic shock requiring 
dobutamine in ten patients [16]. A lower heart rate (9 ±8 
bpm; p< 0.01), a higher stroke volume (10 ±23 ml; p 0.03) 
a longer ultrasound E – A duration (75 ±67 ms; p< 0.01)

and diastolic deceleration time (36 ±42 ms; p< 0.01) 
were reported. Also, cardiac power output was reduced 
(−0.17± 0.23; p< 0.015).
Ivabradine efficacy in rate control was assessed in a 
case series involving six patients who presented with cardiogenic shock and required veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) support, alongside 
persistent tachycardia [14]. Following ivabradine administration, a substantial reduction in heart rate (- 20.83 
bpm; −27.2 to −14.4; p< 0.01) was recorded, along with 
an increase in stroke volume (+ 7.83 ml; 4.74 −10.93; p< 
0.01) and cardiac index (0.83; 0.67–1; p< 0.01), which 
was sufficient to allow for ECMO flow reduction (−0.2 l/
min; −0.31 to −008; p< 0.01).
Nuding et  al. [18] examined the impact of ivabradine 
on a diverse cohort of 70 ICU and coronary unit patients 
who presented with multiorgan dysfunction, defined by 
an APACHE score higher than 20 and a heart rate exceeding 90 beats per minute. The study reported no significant change in heart rate between the intervention and

control groups, and no observable hemodynamic effect. 
Additionally, there were no differences in major adverse 
cardiac events (MACEs) or mortality rates between the 
two groups.
Discussion

In this systematic review, we have reported the existing 
evidence on the use of ivabradine in critically ill patients 
requiring ICU admission for different clinical conditions. 
Persistent tachycardia in the absence of left ventricular 
systolic dysfunction is a common occurrence during septic shock and is often attributed to excessive native and 
pharmacologic adrenergic stimulation, which may lead 
to increased myocardial oxygen demand and the risk of 
ischemia [22]. Catecholamines, although essential for the 
treatment of shock, partially contribute to the worsening 
of systemic inflammation [23]. Prolonged exposure promotes desensitization, leading to the need for increasingly higher doses to achieve the same hemodynamic 
goals and consequently increasing the risk of side effects 
[24]. Therapeutic options such as ivabradine could help 
limit adrenergic stress on the heart, potentially contributing to improved outcomes.
The use of ivabradine led to a significant reduction in 
heart rate (mean difference 18.70 bpm [12.60; 24.80]) 
without a significant decrease in cardiac index in the 
studies included in the meta-analysis. The resolution of 
inappropriate tachycardia likely increased the diastolic 
filling time, allowing stroke volume to rise and resulting 
in a reduction in cardiac workload, and cardiac stress. A 
better cardiac efficiency was associated to vasopressor 
dose reduction in one study [14]. Other studies did not 
consistently report vasopressor dose.
The mean heart rate reduction with ivabradine was 
comparable to that reported in previous studies using 
esmolol [25], suggesting a non-inferior negative chronotropic effect of ivabradine over beta-blockers, without 
any negative inotropic effect. Additionally, ivabradine 
therapy is significantly more cost-effective compared to 
prolonged esmolol infusion, making it a more affordable option, and can be used in association with dobutamine infusion, since it works on different receptors. 
While these results are intriguing, further validation is 
necessary. A phase II clinical trial is currently underway 
in France, involving more than 400 patients, to assess

the effects of ivabradine as an adjuvant therapy in septic 
shock (NCT04031573).
Dobutamine is an inotropic drug used in post-cardiac 
surgery low cardiac output syndrome. As a β1 and partially β2 adrenergic agonist, dobutamine exerts positive

inotropic and chronotropic effects, leading to an increase 
in cardiac output but also higher myocardial oxygen 
demand, peripheral vasodilation and arrythmias [26]. In 
such population, ivabradine could rapidly reduce heart 
rate, with increased cardiac output and systolic blood 
pressure.
In patients with cardiogenic shock [13], ivabradine 
could reduce heart rate and was associated with an 
increase in blood pressure and left ventricular ejection 
fraction. The ivabradine treatment was initiated during 
the acute phase and continued chronically to evaluate its 
long-term effects. There was no statistically significant 
difference in hospital mortality, but the study was not 
powered to investigate this outcome. The mean heart rate 
at baseline in both groups was around 84 bpm, despite 
inotrope infusion, Moreover, using a heart rate cut-off of 
75 bpm to define tachycardia may be too low to identify 
patients affected by excessive adrenergic stimulation.
Similar results are reported by Gallet et  al. [16] In a 
cohort of ten patients ivabradine induced heart rate 
reduction and improved diastolic function and contractile reserve, evaluated by echocardiography. These 
changes were accompanied by better peripheral perfusion in absence of significant changes in cardiac output.

Other outcomes were not assessed.
Limited data on the use of ivabradine in patients with 
cardiogenic shock and requiring veno-arterial ECMO 
support are available. Currently, a clinical trial is underway to investigate the use of ivabradine as an adjunct 
therapy in patients with cardiogenic shock (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03387605).
Of ten studies, just one reported a higher rate of 
adverse events in the treatment group [26]. Five 
patients (36%) developed atrial fibrillation versus none 
in the control group. Sample size was too small to 
determine an association between ivabradine treatment 
and occurrence of de novo atrial fibrillation. Long-term 
administration of ivabradine in patients with chronic 
heart failure has been associated with an increased risk 
of episodes of supraventricular arrhythmias after prolonged use [27]. Yet a short-term use during the first 4 
to 6 days of critical illness has been generally recommended. Few episodes of bradycardia were reported in 
the trial, and they were resolved upon drug discontinuation without adverse consequences. Notably, bradycardia was defined as a heart rate lower than 75 bpm in 
the study, and no severe bradycardia leading to hemodynamic instability was observed. Ivabradine induced 
severe bradycardia has been mainly reported in cases 
of ivabradine overdose or co-ingestion with other heart 
rate lowering drugs, with an average heart rate of 45 to 
50 bpm reported [28]. The other studies did not report 
any episode of bradycardia requiring treatment. Adequate short-term dosing not in association with other 
drugs that reduce heart rate, appears to be quite safe in 
the included studies.
According to the existing evidence, use of 10 mg of 
ivabradine bolus per os followed by 2.5 to 5 mg twice a 
day, up to 7.5 mg twice a day may be effective in controlling inappropriate sinus tachycardia during septic, cardiogenic shock and LCOS following cardiac surgery, even in 
presence of dobutamine infusion. Treatment may last 4 to

6 days according to clinical response (Tables 1 and 2).
Overall, evidence regarding the use of ivabradine in the 
intensive care setting remains limited. Most of the available data are preliminary and derived from small cohorts 
with high heterogeneity. The inconsistency of outcomes 
and endpoints limits the comparability of the studies. 
Furthermore, the studies primarily focus on short-term 
hemodynamic effects, making it difficult to draw conclusions about long-term outcomes.
Conclusions
Ivabradine may be a useful alternative to beta-blocker in 
the management of inappropriate sinus tachycardia during septic, cardiogenic shock and LCOS after cardiac 
surgery even in association to dobutamine. Yet, evidence 
is limited and inconsistent. Larger randomized trials 
are needed to investigate the potential benefits or hazards of ivabradine use on hemodynamics and long-term 
outcomes.
